name: wabt
why: WebAssembly binary toolkit that lets you disassemble, inspect, and rewrite .wasm binaries into readable text and back.

brief.what_it_is: WABT (the WebAssembly Binary Toolkit) is a suite of command-line tools for working with WebAssembly files. It converts the text format (.wat/.wast) to the binary format (.wasm) with wat2wasm and back again with wasm2wat, and it can disassemble and inspect binaries with wasm-objdump and wasm-stats. It can also validate, strip sections from, and interpret binaries (wasm-interp, spectest-interp), convert binaries to C with wasm2c, and convert spec test files to JSON with wast2json. Inputs are .wat, .wast, .wasm, and spec-test JSON files; outputs are binaries, text, C source, JSON, or console reports.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says these tools are "intended for use in (or for development of) toolchains or other systems that want to manipulate WebAssembly files." They are written in C/C++ so they are easier to integrate than the spec interpreter, and they aim for full spec fidelity rather than optimization.
brief.how_it_works: Each tool is a separate executable built from one C/C++ codebase. The README says the tools aim for "1:1 round-trips with no changes to instructions," so converting a binary to text and back should preserve the instructions. The project also says it has been compiled to JavaScript with emscripten to power the online demos.

brief.install_notes: Prebuilt packages: brew install wabt on Homebrew, sudo apt install wabt on apt-based Linux, or download binaries from the GitHub releases page. To build from source you need CMake, plus Ninja if using the top-level Makefile. Clone with --recursive, or run git submodule update --init afterward, to get the test submodules. For CMake directly, create a separate build directory, because running cmake from the repo root will not work. On Windows you need CMake and either Visual Studio 2015 or newer or MinGW. Building gperf is only needed if you add new lexer keywords.
brief.standout: Unlike Binaryen, which is an optimizer and higher-level compiler target, WABT is built for fidelity: it promises byte-exact, instruction-preserving round-trips and treats the spec as the target. The proposal table tracks which WebAssembly proposals each tool supports, with a flag for each, so you can see exactly which features are on by default.
brief.status: unknown. The README has a passing CI badge and a proposal table that includes recent proposals such as wide-arithmetic and custom-page-sizes, but it shows no release date or last-commit date, and I did not fetch the releases page to check.
brief.caveats: The README warns that the top-level Makefile may not build properly on some systems, typically macOS; in that case use CMake directly. The build needs CMake and sometimes Ninja. Threads support must be enabled with --enable-threads and is off by default. Several proposals (threads, custom-page-sizes, compact-imports, function-references, wide-arithmetic) are not default-on, and some are not supported by interpret or wasm2c. The README has no explicit licence statement, and I did not check the LICENSE file.

judge.reason: WABT makes WebAssembly binaries inspectable and executable, with faithful text round-trips that expose the format and its spec rather than merely hiding it behind a compiler.

entry.title: wabt
entry.tldr: A suite of command-line tools that turns WebAssembly binaries into readable text and back, with byte-exact round-trips, so you can see what a .wasm file contains.
entry.deeper_look:
WABT (pronounced "wabbit") is a set of separate executables built from one C/C++ codebase. `wat2wasm` assembles WebAssembly's text format into a binary, and `wasm2wat` goes the other way. `wasm-objdump` and `wasm-stats` inspect a binary, `wasm-validate` checks it, `wasm-strip` removes sections, and `wasm-interp` runs it. `wasm2c` converts a binary to C source, and `wast2json` converts spec test files to JSON.

The project says its tools are "intended for use in (or for development of) toolchains or other systems that want to manipulate WebAssembly files." That is the practical reason it exists, but it also works as a way to look inside WebAssembly. WebAssembly is a compact stack-machine binary format, and `wat2wasm` with `-v` prints the meaning of every byte as it writes the file. Writing a few lines of text, assembling them, and reading the bytes shows how the format is laid out.

The design goal is fidelity rather than cleverness. The README says: "Unlike Binaryen these tools do not aim to provide an optimization platform or a higher-level compiler target; instead they aim for full fidelity and compliance with the spec (e.g. 1:1 round-trips with no changes to instructions)." So a binary converted to text and back should keep its instructions intact, which makes the output trustworthy for inspection.

The project has also been compiled to JavaScript with emscripten to power online demos, so you can try some of the conversions in a browser first.
entry.install:
brew install wabt
# Linux (apt): sudo apt install wabt
# Prebuilt binaries are also on the GitHub releases page.

entry.whats_unique: It aims for spec fidelity and instruction-preserving round-trips rather than optimization, which separates it from Binaryen. A proposal table lists which WebAssembly features each tool supports.
entry.caveats: Several proposals, including threads, are not on by default, and some are not supported by every tool; if you build from source, the top-level Makefile may fail on macOS, so use CMake directly.
